    Model assumptions and cryptographic boundaries
    • Balances, attack routes, settlement and approvals are local teaching models with no bank, wallet or blockchain connection. Posting is assumed atomic: a rejected request causes no debit.
    • Real computation: ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signatures, AES-GCM encryption and authenticated decryption, and SHA-256 block hashes. The AES-GCM teaching channel is not a complete TLS protocol.
    • Signatures and hashes do not encrypt blocks. Encryption hides content; signatures bind payment bytes; hash links expose historical changes. A real network also needs consensus, which this model does not implement.
    • Flipping ciphertext bytes causes authentication failure; it cannot steer encrypted content to a chosen new recipient. In plaintext mode, the attacker replaces the recipient while keeping the original signature.
    • Signer misuse assumes a compromised payment endpoint can invoke signing and session-encryption capabilities. It does not crack algorithms, export private keys or penetrate an uncompromised channel. Independent approval is a Boolean rule with a separate uncompromised trust boundary and exact approved-byte matching.
    • Replay preserves ciphertext, nonce and signature. Authenticated encryption and signatures alone do not prevent business-level replay. This model posts the first request before checking the second.
    • Final blocks store admitted payment data and teaching receipts. Green hashes mean local consistency only. Risk models and quantum comparisons are labeled separately.

    The guided experiment, free-exploration tools and two redacted papers remain available. Explore quantum threats and migration planning using the tabs above.

      Experiment 02 / Tamper evidence

      Follow the chain of evidence.

      Inspect a block. Alter its contents. Recompute hashes. Discover why hash links alone do not establish consensus.
      TOY LEDGER · REAL SHA-256

      Local ledger

      3 BLOCKS
      Append re-verifies the current transaction and signature, then rejects duplicate signed payloads. This is an educational rule, not a production consensus protocol.

      Block inspector

      Changing block data breaks its digest. Rehashing can rebuild a locally consistent history. Real networks also need consensus, replicated state and an agreed history; “hashed” does not mean “immutable”. Public blockchains do not inherently provide transaction confidentiality. Fees and finality depend on the network; the original paper’s blanket comparisons should not be generalized.

      Research update / read the original critically

      The 2022 group paper is preserved as a historical source. Its explanation connecting the Riemann hypothesis to breaking RSA is incorrect. Shor’s algorithm attacks integer factorization and discrete logarithms on a sufficiently capable quantum computer; it does not depend on proving the Riemann hypothesis. Quantum computers do not simply reveal every possible answer at once.

      NIST finalized ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in 2024. “Quantum resistant” describes confidence under known attacks, not a proof against every future attack. This lab assigns no date to a cryptographically relevant quantum computer.

      Primary sources: NIST FIPS 204 · NIST FIPS 205 · Shor, factoring and discrete logarithms

      Experiment 05 / From experiment to decision

      Design a migration, not a countdown.

      Change your constraints to prioritize a signature migration. Outputs are transparent teaching heuristics, not a security assessment or mandated schedule.
      ILLUSTRATIVE DECISION SUPPORT

      System constraints

      No inputs leave this browser. Signature longevity is different from “harvest now, decrypt later”, which concerns confidentiality and key establishment.

      Recommended next move

      Decision rules

      Priority is higher when lifetime + lead time ≥ 15 years, otherwise planned migration. Missing inventory always makes discovery the first step. Diversity selects an SLH-DSA pilot; otherwise ML-DSA. A bandwidth constraint adds a payload feasibility gate. These cutoffs are authored for this demo and predict no quantum arrival date.
